meta.title: Why safe retries need **idempotency**
meta.subject: Making payment webhooks safe to retry
meta.one_liner: Retrying is easy. Retrying without doing things twice is the real trick.

goal: By the end you can explain why trying again can charge a customer twice, and the two ideas that stop it.
hook: Apps resend messages all the time when the internet hiccups. So why don't you get charged twice every time it happens?

concepts.name: Retries with backoff
concepts.tagline: If at first you don't succeed, wait a bit longer and try again.
concepts.explain:
Messages between computers get lost or delayed all the time. When a sender hears nothing back, it can't tell "it failed" from "it worked but the reply got lost", so it plays safe and **sends again**.

Good senders wait longer after each failure: 1 second, then 2, then 4. This is called **backoff**, and it stops a struggling server from being buried under repeats.
concepts.product: Retries are why payments, emails and alerts still arrive when the internet has a bad moment. The cost: the same message can arrive more than once.
concepts.tech: Senders retry on timeouts and server errors, adding random jitter so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep. Delivery is "at least once", never "exactly once".

examples.title: Calling a friend
examples.text: No answer? You call again in a few minutes, not every second. That pause is backoff.

examples.title: Payment providers
examples.text: Payment platforms resend failed notifications for hours or days, with growing gaps between tries.

in_your_work.text: Your payment provider sent the same payment notice twice because your app took too long to reply.

concepts.pitfall: Assuming each message arrives exactly once. With retries, "at least once" is the honest promise.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.tagline: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
concepts.explain:
An action is **idempotent** when repeating it changes nothing after the first time. "Mark the order as paid" is idempotent. "Add ₹500 to the balance" is not.

The usual trick: every request carries a **unique ID**. The receiver remembers IDs it has handled, and when one shows up again it simply skips the work.
concepts.product: Customers never see double charges, duplicate emails or two identical orders, even when the network misbehaves. A good question for any engineer: "what happens if this arrives twice?"
concepts.tech: Store a record keyed by the request or event ID. Look the key up before acting; if it exists, return the saved result instead of redoing the work.

examples.title: The lift button
examples.text: Pressing it five times still calls one lift.

examples.title: Payment APIs
examples.text: Major payment APIs accept an idempotency key, so a retried charge never runs twice.

code.caption: The idea, simplified

in_your_work.text: Your payment handler now remembers every payment notice it has seen and ignores repeats.

concepts.pitfall: Making a new ID for each retry. A repeat must carry the same ID as the original, or nobody can recognise it.

concepts.name: Check and act in one step
concepts.tagline: "Have I done this?" and "do it" must happen together.
concepts.explain:
If two copies of the same message arrive at the **same moment**, both can ask "seen this before?", both hear "no", and both act.

The fix is to make the check and the action one **indivisible step**. Databases offer this: a rule that a given ID can only be saved once, checked in the same step as the work.
concepts.product: This is the difference between "usually no duplicates" and "never duplicates". It matters most for money, stock levels and anything customers see.
concepts.tech: Insert the ID into a table with a unique index inside the same transaction as the business write. The second insert fails, and its transaction rolls back.

examples.title: The last concert ticket
examples.text: Two fans click Buy at the same instant. Exactly one of them can get it, never both.

examples.title: Seat booking
examples.text: Airlines and cinemas lock a seat in the same step as selling it, so it can't be sold twice.

steps.label: Both try to save the ID

in_your_work.text: Saving the notice's ID and updating the order now happen as one step in your database.

quiz.question: A server did the work but crashed before replying. What will a well-behaved sender do?

options.why: The sender never got a reply, so it can't know that.

options.text: Send the same message again after a pause
options.why: No reply looks like failure, so it retries with backoff.

options.text: Send a brand-new message with a new ID
options.why: Retries resend the same message. A new ID would hide that it's a repeat.

quiz.question: Which of these actions is idempotent?

options.text: Add one item to the cart
options.why: Doing it twice leaves two items.

options.text: Set the user's plan to Pro
options.why: After the first time, repeating it changes nothing.

quiz.question: Two copies of one payment arrive at the same millisecond. What stops a double charge?

options.why: Timing tricks shrink the gap; they don't close it.

options.text: Saving the ID and charging in one indivisible step
options.why: Only one save can succeed, so only one charge happens.
Logs record the duplicate after it happens.

share.linkedin:
Learned something today that explains a lot of "charged twice" bugs.

Apps resend messages whenever the internet hiccups, so the same message can arrive more than once. The fix is idempotency: design actions so doing them twice has the same effect as once.

And the check has to happen in the same step as the work, or two simultaneous repeats can still slip through.
